title: Worlds 2026 and the Demon King’s Unfinished Story
subtitle: Faker chases a seventh title as Worlds returns to North America with a larger field and an unpredictable race for the Cup.
paragraphs: Watching Faker at Worlds 2026 feels like watching Tom Brady in his final years with the Patriots. His place as the greatest is already secure, but he’s still chasing championships. Every run leaves fans wondering how many more times they’ll get to see him compete for another title.

Lee “Faker” Sang-hyeok has won six world championships. T1’s victories in 2023, 2024 and 2025 made them the first team to win three consecutive Worlds titles. A victory this year would give him his seventh crown and extend that streak to four.
For everyone challenging T1, this tournament offers the opportunity to end a reign that has defined the last three Worlds.
Familiar Ground and New Stakes
Nineteen teams entered Worlds 2026, up from 17 last year. The tournament began in Los Angeles before moving to Allen, Texas, with the final scheduled for November 14 at Barclays Center in Brooklyn.
American soil carries some history for Faker. He won his third world title in Los Angeles in 2016. In 2022, T1 lost a five-game final to DRX in San Francisco.

Those two tournaments captured very different moments in his career. One cemented an early dynasty; the other left him one victory short of ending a championship drought. Ten years after that Los Angeles triumph, he has a chance to leave another American Worlds with his seventh title.

This year’s competition has already delivered a reminder of how quickly championship expectations can collapse. Hanwha Life Esports, the reigning Mid-Season Invitational champions, were eliminated by Bilibili Gaming in the Swiss Stage. Their 2–0 defeat made them the first MSI-winning team to miss the Worlds knockout stage in the same year.
Even a major international trophy won a few months earlier could not secure them a place in the quarterfinals.
The Challengers Have Their Own Stories

Gen.G and Dplus KIA finished Swiss with unbeaten 3–0 records, while T1 advanced at 3–1. The quarterfinal field includes three Korean teams and three Chinese teams, alongside Europe’s Karmine Corp and North America’s LYON.

Karmine Corp have made the quarterfinals on their first Worlds appearance, having started in the Play-In Stage. Their next opponent, on November 6, is T1. For KC, the biggest moment in the organization’s Worlds history will mean facing the tournament’s most decorated player.
LYON, meanwhile, face Gen.G on November 4, carrying North America’s remaining hopes at a tournament hosted in the United States.

The games themselves also present a different test from Faker’s early championships. Fearless Draft, introduced at Worlds in 2025, continues this year: once either team selects a champion, neither can use it again during that series. By Game 5, 40 previously played champions are unavailable before the regular bans even begin.
That can turn a deciding game into a test of how deep a team’s preparation goes. A signature pick might help win the opener, but the players need other answers as the series progresses.
What More Does the Demon King Have to Prove?
Faker’s six titles span two distinct championship runs: 2013, 2015 and 2016, then 2023, 2024 and 2025. Seven years separated his third and fourth crowns.
That return is central to his GOAT status. His career includes early dominance, years of falling short at Worlds, and another run of championships after the game and his teammates had changed.
Riot made him its first Hall of Legends inductee in 2024, when he had four world titles. He has added two more since the game began celebrating his legacy.
At 30, he remains contracted to T1 through 2029. This Worlds has not been announced as his farewell, and there may be several chapters still ahead.

Brady offered a memorable example of that possibility. After leaving New England, he won his seventh Super Bowl with Tampa Bay at 43. A career that already seemed complete still had another championship in it.
Faker has already explained why his own pursuit continues. Speaking in December 2025, he said: “If I have to prove something, it has to be to myself.”

His place in League history can be secure while another Worlds still matters intensely. In 2026, he has the chance to extend an unprecedented streak. His opponents have the chance to be remembered as the team that stopped it.
That is enough to make this Worlds worth watching, however much longer the Demon King’s career lasts.
